Federaţia arată că, potrivit unui proiect de ordin discutat în şedinţa Comisiei de Dialog Social, Ministerul Educaţiei a propus menţinerea cuantumul minim al bursei sociale la 925 de lei.

medical.title: Cancer drug pushes mutant blood stem cells to become short-lived immune cells
medical.summary: The biologic drug interferon-alpha can benefit patients with blood cancers called myeloproliferative neoplasms by forcing mutant blood stem cells to become shorter-lived white blood cells, according to a study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. Because the broad activity of interferon-alpha can induce significant side effects, developing more focused strategies based on these mechanistic findings could meet an important need in cancer therapy.

medical.title: Strength training 101: A guide to building muscle safely at any age
medical.summary: Strength training is one of the most effective ways to improve your health, boost your metabolism and enhance your quality of life—no matter your age.

medical.title: Dengue‑carrying mosquitoes expand their reach into new territories—including Florida
medical.summary: The Tampa Bay Times reported the death of an older woman on Sept. 8, 2026. Her family says local doctors attributed her death to dengue fever, although the Florida Department of Health has not yet confirmed it.

medical.title: Stopping dying cells from rupturing could help donor livers withstand transplantation
medical.summary: During transplantation, blood flow to the donor liver must stop as it's moved to the recipient. Once transplanted, oxygen-rich blood is restored, yet doing so can cause what is called ischemia-reperfusion injury. To protect transplanted livers from this tissue damage, researchers at The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) have discovered a way to protect dying cells from rupturing and affecting the surrounding area.

medical.title: Daydreams, mind‑wandering and rumination: What you think about can affect your feelings and mood
medical.summary: Numerous types of thoughts pass through your mind over the course of a day. You may be reminiscing about your last vacation, thinking about a news story, recalling a funny conversation or brainstorming ideas for weekend plans. Not only are these thoughts highly prevalent in everyday life, but they also have wide-ranging impacts on how we function.

medical.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation may improve immunotherapy-related colitis
medical.summary: Targeting the gut microbiome with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) may help cancer patients with immunotherapy-related colitis avoid the need for steroids and other immunosuppressive treatments, according to researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

medical.title: How South Korea is tackling its super‑aging problem—and what other aging nations can learn from its experience
medical.summary: In December 2024, the share of South Koreans ages 65 and older surpassed 20% for the first time, making it what demographers like us call a "super-aged society." By August 2026, that share had risen further to 22.1%.

medical.title: Retinal scans may flag atrial fibrillation four years before diagnosis
medical.summary: People with atrial fibrillation have signs of the condition in their retinas that can be detected as early as four years before diagnosis, according to a new study led by University College London (UCL) and Moorfields researchers.

medical.title: Hot, dry weather can make you cough more—salty air might help
medical.summary: UNC School of Medicine researcher Brian Button, Ph.D., professor of biochemistry and biophysics, and collaborators have identified how extremely dry air during heat waves can make the airways more sensitive and more likely to cough, and how a nonpharmacological magnesium salt aerosol may provide relief.

medical.title: Brain blood flow linked to fatigue after COVID-19
medical.summary: Fatigue is one of the most common and disabling symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), often referred to as long COVID. Although the condition has been studied extensively since the pandemic, the biological mechanisms behind persistent symptoms are still not fully understood.

medical.title: AI helps pathologists find signs of preeclampsia, advancing diagnosis and treatment
medical.summary: Preeclampsia is one of the leading causes of pregnancy-related death. Even after a healthy delivery, mother and baby can go home only to show signs of a postpartum hypertensive disorder days or weeks later.

medical.title: Study demonstrates how machine learning model enables targeted Lp(a) screening
medical.summary: The Family Heart Foundation has published a new study in JACC: Advances demonstrating how its FIND Lp(a) Machine Learning Model can identify people with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) who are more likely to have high lipoprotein(a)—or Lp(a).

medical.title: Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
medical.summary: Simply smelling chocolate helped men complete more leg extension repetitions without making the workout feel harder, with dark chocolate producing the strongest effect. The researchers think familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation by making the brain anticipate eating.

medical.title: Investigational immunotherapy nearly doubles overall survival compared with docetaxel in advanced squamous NSCLC
medical.summary: Patients with metastatic squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose disease progressed following PD-(L)1 inhibitor therapy experienced a median overall survival of 18.5 months with the investigational anti-CTLA-4 antibody gotistobart, compared with 10.0 months for patients receiving docetaxel, according to updated findings from stage 1 of the Phase III PRESERVE-003 trial.

medical.title: Experimental cancer vaccine makes its own oxygen and gives T-cells a boost
medical.summary: When it comes to priorities in life, oxygen tops the list. Humans can go weeks without food and days without water. Take away the ability to breathe, however, and the clock starts ticking within minutes as the brain begins shutting down. But the life-giving gas does even more heavy lifting than you might think.

medical.title: Study identifies distinct outcomes and genomic features in NSCLC with class II and III BRAF alterations
medical.summary: Patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring class II and class III BRAF alterations have distinct clinicopathologic and genomic characteristics, with class III alterations potentially associated with worse prognosis, according to research presented at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC).

medical.title: Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization.

medical.title: Why most emergency headache patients disappear into the data
medical.summary: Thousands of people visit emergency departments with headaches every year, but research suggests the way these visits are recorded may be hiding important clues about patients' needs.

medical.title: Where you live may influence your brain health
medical.summary: In a study analyzing nearly 3,000 brain MRI exams, researchers found that living in highly disadvantaged neighborhoods was associated with adverse brain health. Results of the study were published in Radiology.

medical.title: More time on social media means more anxiety, depression for teens—especially girls
medical.summary: Spending more time on social media is making Canadian teenagers—especially girls—feel anxious, depressed and disconnected, according to a study co-led by University of Alberta researchers.

medical.title: Cataract surgery continues to improve across Europe
medical.summary: A total of 363,039 cataract surgeries performed in 12 European countries in 2024 were recorded in the European Registry of Quality Outcomes for Cataract and Refractive Surgery (EUREQUO), according to the latest figures presented at the 44th Congress of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons (ESCRS).

medical.title: Lower breast, cervical cancer screening seen for adults with disabilities
medical.summary: Individuals with disabilities have a lower prevalence of breast and cervical cancer screening, according to a study published in Cancer.

medical.title: Nearly 10,000 patients reveal what works best for knee arthritis pain relief
medical.summary: A major analysis of 139 clinical trials involving nearly 10,000 people suggests that some of the simplest treatments may work best for knee osteoarthritis. Knee braces ranked highest overall for reducing pain, stiffness, and mobility problems, while water-based therapy was especially effective for pain and regular exercise consistently improved both pain and physical function. More high-tech approaches, including ultrasound, generally performed worse.

medical.title: Tiny cell “antennas” may help explain why some babies are born with heart defects
medical.summary: A newly discovered communication system in the microscopic “antennae” of cells may help explain how some congenital heart defects develop. When genetic mutations disrupt this system, the effects may extend beyond the heart to organs including the brain, kidneys, and skeleton.

science.title: Satellite data reveal ESG scores track public image more than actual forest loss
science.summary: Environmental sustainability researchers at NUS found that widely used environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings often fail to reflect companies' actual exposure to deforestation, highlighting the need to integrate satellite-based environmental data into sustainable investing frameworks.

science.title: How individual cells 'surf' chemical waves to form a collective
science.summary: Researchers have developed an innovative imaging technique to visualize the transition of single cells into multicellular organisms in new detail.

science.title: Biophysical model suggests how cells optimize information gathering without using too much energy
science.summary: In both biological and engineered systems, cells and sensors must make sense of noisy, changing signals to function. However, collecting and using this information consumes valuable energy. A new study, published in Physical Review Letters, describes a model for how a sensor or cell might maximize information collection from its surroundings while controlling the overall energy cost, resulting in an optimized system.

science.title: Local experience shapes how coastal communities understand and respond to climate change
science.summary: While people across the globe are experiencing various impacts of climate change, governments and communicators often use top-to-bottom, uniform communication strategies to inform people about climate change.

science.title: Fertilizer study reveals where the world can boost food production and cut pollution
science.summary: Global consumption of fertilizer has doubled since 1980, but some regions that have historically overused fertilizer, including China and parts of Europe, have taken steps to reduce use. Those are some of the findings of a new global dataset from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment.

science.title: New research calls for more consistent, child-centered policing to build trust and protect children
science.summary: New research co-led by the University of Bedfordshire and the University of Lancashire has highlighted the need for more consistent child-centered and safeguarding-led approaches across policing, with children and young people's experiences varying depending on where they live, whom they encounter, the reason for these encounters and how well systems support frontline practice.

science.title: Examining Americans' complicated relationship with science
science.summary: A new study finds that while most Americans are interested in science and believe it benefits society, the public's relationship with science is more complicated than those positive views suggest.

science.title: Celebrate International Observe the Moon Night with NASA
science.summary: In April, the world watched as four humans circled the Moon for the first time in over 50 years with NASA’s Artemis II mission. On Saturday, Sept. 19, the public is invited to look up again with NASA events across the country, including the International Observe the Moon Night celebration held at NASA’s Goddard Space […]

science.summary: NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik (left) and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano view progress on the solid rocket booster integration in High Bay 3 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Bresnik, Parmitano, and NASA astronauts Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and Bob Hines made […]

science.title: Planting trees in the wrong places is not a climate solution
science.summary: A recent United Nations report has stated that the world will likely overshoot the 1.5°C target set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement by 2030.

science.title: Marine bacteria team up to break down one of the ocean's toughest carbon-storing molecules
science.summary: Deep in the ocean, brown algae and diatoms produce a complex carbohydrate molecule called fucoidan, which helps form their protective outer layers. The fucoidan molecule is very difficult for microbes to break down because its chemical structure may include dozens of different linkages and branching patterns that vary from one algal species to another.

science.title: Advanced X-ray crystallography determines structure of macromolecule at unprecedented resolution
science.summary: Proteins are high-performance molecular machines that carry out nearly every biochemical function inside living cells. To understand how they achieve this, scientists often examine their detailed atomic structure, which holds important clues to their activity. The more precision they achieve, the deeper the insight they may gain into the chemical principles that underlie protein structure and, ultimately, function.

science.title: Ancient DNA traces medieval migration from Sweden to Finland
science.summary: A new study led by the University of Turku provides new insights into the population history of Finland during the Late Iron Age and the Middle Ages. The researchers analyzed the genomes of people who lived in southwestern Finland and Häme between the 11th and 13th centuries to investigate how the population changed over the course of the Middle Ages and how people were connected to other regions around the Baltic Sea.

science.title: Europe's e‑waste is a valuable resource—let's not throw it away
science.summary: Throwing something away that is urgently needed, expensive and difficult to source sounds crazy. Yet of the 60 metals contained in old electronic devices such as phones, screens and washing machines, only a few are recycled. That includes precious metals such as gold and silver and other metals such as aluminum and copper. The rest are effectively single-use metals, used once and then lost during collection or through incineration.

science.title: Our new research shows humans have maligned bandicoots for decades, making them more vulnerable to extinction
science.summary: Have you ever found your lawn riddled with holes or heard a little sneeze from your backyard bushes? Those are signs you might have a resident bandicoot. Bandicoots are nocturnal, rabbit-sized marsupials known for their pointy snouts, thin tails and large hind feet. Due to these features, they were originally misnamed after a type of rat from India, the pandi-kokku, or "pig-rat" (Bandicota sp.).

science.title: Laser altimeter BELA ready to explore Mercury's surface
science.summary: Launched on Oct. 20, 2018, the joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has traveled for almost eight years, using a carefully planned but eventful sequence of planetary flybys and solar-electric propulsion to gradually approach its destination, Mercury. The mission is now entering the final stage of its journey to the smallest and innermost planet of our solar system.

science.title: This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
science.summary: Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site.

science.title: A 5,000-year-old royal mystery: Digital clues point to Meretneith as Egypt's female king
science.summary: More than 5,000 years ago, a royal woman named Meretneith (also written as Merneith) lived in ancient Egypt. She was possibly the daughter of Djer, the third king of the First Dynasty, a period when the first kings ruled over a unified Egypt.

science.title: To crack the job market, internships can be just as key for young people as the degree
science.summary: College students are facing one of the most precarious labor markets in years. A recent New York Federal Reserve study pointed to a sharp increase in unemployment among recent college graduates compared with other workers, with explanations ranging from artificial intelligence job displacement to a broader slowdown in hiring.

science.title: Children trust what they hear over what they see, study finds
science.summary: New research from our Department of Psychology has revealed that children are far more likely than adults to judge a person's emotions by what they hear rather than what they see.

science.title: Bubbles the food-stealing dolphin finds shortcut to easy meal
science.summary: A dolphin that harasses fish until they regurgitate their food—then swoops in to steal it—has astonished University of the Sunshine Coast researchers who have documented this novel feeding strategy.

science.title: UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile
science.summary: A 125-million-year-old crocodile fossil has revealed preserved skin, possible sensory organs, sophisticated respiratory structures, and an unexpected pattern on its tail. Ultraviolet light exposed alternating bands that may represent ancient camouflage, potentially preserving the oldest known coloration in a crocodylomorph.

science.title: Invasive little fire ants prefer cooked beef, seeds over tuna
science.summary: If you are trying to detect or bait little fire ants in your backyard, scientists at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa suggest swapping tuna for cooked beef and sunflower seeds. The study, published in the Journal of Applied Entomology by researchers at the UH Mānoa College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience (CTAHR), revealed that the little fire ant's (Wasmannia auropunctata) preferred diet is not what scientists and homeowners previously thought. In laboratory food-choice tests, the tiny, stinging pests overwhelmingly chose cooked beef and sunflower seeds over water-packed tuna.

science.title: Robots and AI uncover unexpected pathway in classic 135-year-old chemical reaction
science.summary: Chemical reactions are often written as simple equations: Starting materials go in, and a product comes out. In reality, the same substrates can follow many different pathways depending on their concentrations, temperature, catalysts and other conditions.

science.title: Young European shags reveal how first winter experiences may guide migration
science.summary: Should I stay or should I go? What determines whether birds migrate for the winter? This is one of the questions explored in a new doctoral thesis by Cassandra Ugland from NTNU's Department of Biology. The work is published in the Journal of Animal Ecology.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: ANOSR: Costul real al vieții de student depășește cu mult bursa socială actuală. Ce schimbări solicită tinerii
mix_items.summary: Alianţa Naţională a Organizaţiilor Studenţeşti din România (ANOSR) solicită ca bursa socială să fie de minim 1.050 de lei, arătând că o analiză făcută în luna ianuarie a indicat că suma care acoperă cheltuielile lunare ale unui student pentru masă şi cazare este de 1.525 de lei. Federaţia arată că, potrivit unui proiect de ordin discutat în şedinţa Comisiei de Dialog Social, Ministerul Educaţiei a propus menţinerea cuantumul minim al bursei sociale la 925 de lei.

mix_items.summary: CashClub, platforma de cashback și cumpărături inteligente, lansează o versiune nouă a site-ului și a aplicației mobile, după trei luni de dezvoltare și o investiție de 20.000 de euro, acoperită...

mix_items.title: Cancer drug pushes mutant blood stem cells to become short-lived immune cells
mix_items.summary: The biologic drug interferon-alpha can benefit patients with blood cancers called myeloproliferative neoplasms by forcing mutant blood stem cells to become shorter-lived white blood cells, according to a study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. Because the broad activity of interferon-alpha can induce significant side effects, developing more focused strategies based on these mechanistic findings could meet an important need in cancer therapy.

mix_items.title: Satellite data reveal ESG scores track public image more than actual forest loss
mix_items.summary: Environmental sustainability researchers at NUS found that widely used environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings often fail to reflect companies' actual exposure to deforestation, highlighting the need to integrate satellite-based environmental data into sustainable investing frameworks.

mix_items.title: Strength training 101: A guide to building muscle safely at any age
mix_items.summary: Strength training is one of the most effective ways to improve your health, boost your metabolism and enhance your quality of life—no matter your age.

mix_items.title: Dengue‑carrying mosquitoes expand their reach into new territories—including Florida
mix_items.summary: The Tampa Bay Times reported the death of an older woman on Sept. 8, 2026. Her family says local doctors attributed her death to dengue fever, although the Florida Department of Health has not yet confirmed it.

mix_items.title: How individual cells 'surf' chemical waves to form a collective
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed an innovative imaging technique to visualize the transition of single cells into multicellular organisms in new detail.

mix_items.title: Stopping dying cells from rupturing could help donor livers withstand transplantation
mix_items.summary: During transplantation, blood flow to the donor liver must stop as it's moved to the recipient. Once transplanted, oxygen-rich blood is restored, yet doing so can cause what is called ischemia-reperfusion injury. To protect transplanted livers from this tissue damage, researchers at The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) have discovered a way to protect dying cells from rupturing and affecting the surrounding area.

mix_items.title: Biophysical model suggests how cells optimize information gathering without using too much energy
mix_items.summary: In both biological and engineered systems, cells and sensors must make sense of noisy, changing signals to function. However, collecting and using this information consumes valuable energy. A new study, published in Physical Review Letters, describes a model for how a sensor or cell might maximize information collection from its surroundings while controlling the overall energy cost, resulting in an optimized system.

mix_items.title: Daydreams, mind‑wandering and rumination: What you think about can affect your feelings and mood
mix_items.summary: Numerous types of thoughts pass through your mind over the course of a day. You may be reminiscing about your last vacation, thinking about a news story, recalling a funny conversation or brainstorming ideas for weekend plans. Not only are these thoughts highly prevalent in everyday life, but they also have wide-ranging impacts on how we function.

mix_items.title: Local experience shapes how coastal communities understand and respond to climate change
mix_items.summary: While people across the globe are experiencing various impacts of climate change, governments and communicators often use top-to-bottom, uniform communication strategies to inform people about climate change.

mix_items.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation may improve immunotherapy-related colitis
mix_items.summary: Targeting the gut microbiome with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) may help cancer patients with immunotherapy-related colitis avoid the need for steroids and other immunosuppressive treatments, according to researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Fertilizer study reveals where the world can boost food production and cut pollution
mix_items.summary: Global consumption of fertilizer has doubled since 1980, but some regions that have historically overused fertilizer, including China and parts of Europe, have taken steps to reduce use. Those are some of the findings of a new global dataset from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment.

mix_items.title: How South Korea is tackling its super‑aging problem—and what other aging nations can learn from its experience
mix_items.summary: In December 2024, the share of South Koreans ages 65 and older surpassed 20% for the first time, making it what demographers like us call a "super-aged society." By August 2026, that share had risen further to 22.1%.

mix_items.title: New research calls for more consistent, child-centered policing to build trust and protect children
mix_items.summary: New research co-led by the University of Bedfordshire and the University of Lancashire has highlighted the need for more consistent child-centered and safeguarding-led approaches across policing, with children and young people's experiences varying depending on where they live, whom they encounter, the reason for these encounters and how well systems support frontline practice.

mix_items.title: Examining Americans' complicated relationship with science
mix_items.summary: A new study finds that while most Americans are interested in science and believe it benefits society, the public's relationship with science is more complicated than those positive views suggest.

mix_items.title: Retinal scans may flag atrial fibrillation four years before diagnosis
mix_items.summary: People with atrial fibrillation have signs of the condition in their retinas that can be detected as early as four years before diagnosis, according to a new study led by University College London (UCL) and Moorfields researchers.

mix_items.title: Celebrate International Observe the Moon Night with NASA
mix_items.summary: In April, the world watched as four humans circled the Moon for the first time in over 50 years with NASA’s Artemis II mission. On Saturday, Sept. 19, the public is invited to look up again with NASA events across the country, including the International Observe the Moon Night celebration held at NASA’s Goddard Space […]

mix_items.summary: NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik (left) and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano view progress on the solid rocket booster integration in High Bay 3 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Bresnik, Parmitano, and NASA astronauts Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and Bob Hines made […]

mix_items.title: Planting trees in the wrong places is not a climate solution
mix_items.summary: A recent United Nations report has stated that the world will likely overshoot the 1.5°C target set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement by 2030.

mix_items.title: Hot, dry weather can make you cough more—salty air might help
mix_items.summary: UNC School of Medicine researcher Brian Button, Ph.D., professor of biochemistry and biophysics, and collaborators have identified how extremely dry air during heat waves can make the airways more sensitive and more likely to cough, and how a nonpharmacological magnesium salt aerosol may provide relief.

mix_items.title: Marine bacteria team up to break down one of the ocean's toughest carbon-storing molecules
mix_items.summary: Deep in the ocean, brown algae and diatoms produce a complex carbohydrate molecule called fucoidan, which helps form their protective outer layers. The fucoidan molecule is very difficult for microbes to break down because its chemical structure may include dozens of different linkages and branching patterns that vary from one algal species to another.

mix_items.title: Brain blood flow linked to fatigue after COVID-19
mix_items.summary: Fatigue is one of the most common and disabling symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), often referred to as long COVID. Although the condition has been studied extensively since the pandemic, the biological mechanisms behind persistent symptoms are still not fully understood.

mix_items.title: AI helps pathologists find signs of preeclampsia, advancing diagnosis and treatment
mix_items.summary: Preeclampsia is one of the leading causes of pregnancy-related death. Even after a healthy delivery, mother and baby can go home only to show signs of a postpartum hypertensive disorder days or weeks later.

mix_items.title: Advanced X-ray crystallography determines structure of macromolecule at unprecedented resolution
mix_items.summary: Proteins are high-performance molecular machines that carry out nearly every biochemical function inside living cells. To understand how they achieve this, scientists often examine their detailed atomic structure, which holds important clues to their activity. The more precision they achieve, the deeper the insight they may gain into the chemical principles that underlie protein structure and, ultimately, function.

mix_items.title: Study demonstrates how machine learning model enables targeted Lp(a) screening
mix_items.summary: The Family Heart Foundation has published a new study in JACC: Advances demonstrating how its FIND Lp(a) Machine Learning Model can identify people with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) who are more likely to have high lipoprotein(a)—or Lp(a).

mix_items.title: Ancient DNA traces medieval migration from Sweden to Finland
mix_items.summary: A new study led by the University of Turku provides new insights into the population history of Finland during the Late Iron Age and the Middle Ages. The researchers analyzed the genomes of people who lived in southwestern Finland and Häme between the 11th and 13th centuries to investigate how the population changed over the course of the Middle Ages and how people were connected to other regions around the Baltic Sea.

mix_items.title: Europe's e‑waste is a valuable resource—let's not throw it away
mix_items.summary: Throwing something away that is urgently needed, expensive and difficult to source sounds crazy. Yet of the 60 metals contained in old electronic devices such as phones, screens and washing machines, only a few are recycled. That includes precious metals such as gold and silver and other metals such as aluminum and copper. The rest are effectively single-use metals, used once and then lost during collection or through incineration.

mix_items.title: Smelling chocolate helped men complete more reps without feeling more tired
mix_items.summary: Simply smelling chocolate helped men complete more leg extension repetitions without making the workout feel harder, with dark chocolate producing the strongest effect. The researchers think familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation by making the brain anticipate eating.

mix_items.title: Investigational immunotherapy nearly doubles overall survival compared with docetaxel in advanced squamous NSCLC
mix_items.summary: Patients with metastatic squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose disease progressed following PD-(L)1 inhibitor therapy experienced a median overall survival of 18.5 months with the investigational anti-CTLA-4 antibody gotistobart, compared with 10.0 months for patients receiving docetaxel, according to updated findings from stage 1 of the Phase III PRESERVE-003 trial.

mix_items.title: Our new research shows humans have maligned bandicoots for decades, making them more vulnerable to extinction
mix_items.summary: Have you ever found your lawn riddled with holes or heard a little sneeze from your backyard bushes? Those are signs you might have a resident bandicoot. Bandicoots are nocturnal, rabbit-sized marsupials known for their pointy snouts, thin tails and large hind feet. Due to these features, they were originally misnamed after a type of rat from India, the pandi-kokku, or "pig-rat" (Bandicota sp.).

mix_items.title: Experimental cancer vaccine makes its own oxygen and gives T-cells a boost
mix_items.summary: When it comes to priorities in life, oxygen tops the list. Humans can go weeks without food and days without water. Take away the ability to breathe, however, and the clock starts ticking within minutes as the brain begins shutting down. But the life-giving gas does even more heavy lifting than you might think.

mix_items.title: Laser altimeter BELA ready to explore Mercury's surface
mix_items.summary: Launched on Oct. 20, 2018, the joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has traveled for almost eight years, using a carefully planned but eventful sequence of planetary flybys and solar-electric propulsion to gradually approach its destination, Mercury. The mission is now entering the final stage of its journey to the smallest and innermost planet of our solar system.

mix_items.title: This Australian cave hid 25,000 years of ritual secrets
mix_items.summary: Microscopic plant remains are revealing how GunaiKurnai ancestors used Cloggs Cave for ritual practices over thousands of years. People deliberately gathered whole grasses, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers, leaving behind traces that may span 25,000 years. A standing stone erected around 2,000 years ago and other ritual objects strengthen the evidence that the cave was a long-lived spiritual site.

mix_items.title: Study identifies distinct outcomes and genomic features in NSCLC with class II and III BRAF alterations
mix_items.summary: Patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring class II and class III BRAF alterations have distinct clinicopathologic and genomic characteristics, with class III alterations potentially associated with worse prognosis, according to research presented at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC).

mix_items.title: A 5,000-year-old royal mystery: Digital clues point to Meretneith as Egypt's female king
mix_items.summary: More than 5,000 years ago, a royal woman named Meretneith (also written as Merneith) lived in ancient Egypt. She was possibly the daughter of Djer, the third king of the First Dynasty, a period when the first kings ruled over a unified Egypt.

mix_items.title: To crack the job market, internships can be just as key for young people as the degree
mix_items.summary: College students are facing one of the most precarious labor markets in years. A recent New York Federal Reserve study pointed to a sharp increase in unemployment among recent college graduates compared with other workers, with explanations ranging from artificial intelligence job displacement to a broader slowdown in hiring.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization.

mix_items.title: Children trust what they hear over what they see, study finds
mix_items.summary: New research from our Department of Psychology has revealed that children are far more likely than adults to judge a person's emotions by what they hear rather than what they see.

mix_items.title: Bubbles the food-stealing dolphin finds shortcut to easy meal
mix_items.summary: A dolphin that harasses fish until they regurgitate their food—then swoops in to steal it—has astonished University of the Sunshine Coast researchers who have documented this novel feeding strategy.

mix_items.title: Why most emergency headache patients disappear into the data
mix_items.summary: Thousands of people visit emergency departments with headaches every year, but research suggests the way these visits are recorded may be hiding important clues about patients' needs.

mix_items.title: UV light reveals possible camouflage on a 125-million-year-old crocodile
mix_items.summary: A 125-million-year-old crocodile fossil has revealed preserved skin, possible sensory organs, sophisticated respiratory structures, and an unexpected pattern on its tail. Ultraviolet light exposed alternating bands that may represent ancient camouflage, potentially preserving the oldest known coloration in a crocodylomorph.

mix_items.title: Where you live may influence your brain health
mix_items.summary: In a study analyzing nearly 3,000 brain MRI exams, researchers found that living in highly disadvantaged neighborhoods was associated with adverse brain health. Results of the study were published in Radiology.

mix_items.title: Invasive little fire ants prefer cooked beef, seeds over tuna
mix_items.summary: If you are trying to detect or bait little fire ants in your backyard, scientists at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa suggest swapping tuna for cooked beef and sunflower seeds. The study, published in the Journal of Applied Entomology by researchers at the UH Mānoa College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience (CTAHR), revealed that the little fire ant's (Wasmannia auropunctata) preferred diet is not what scientists and homeowners previously thought. In laboratory food-choice tests, the tiny, stinging pests overwhelmingly chose cooked beef and sunflower seeds over water-packed tuna.

mix_items.title: Robots and AI uncover unexpected pathway in classic 135-year-old chemical reaction
mix_items.summary: Chemical reactions are often written as simple equations: Starting materials go in, and a product comes out. In reality, the same substrates can follow many different pathways depending on their concentrations, temperature, catalysts and other conditions.

mix_items.title: Young European shags reveal how first winter experiences may guide migration
mix_items.summary: Should I stay or should I go? What determines whether birds migrate for the winter? This is one of the questions explored in a new doctoral thesis by Cassandra Ugland from NTNU's Department of Biology. The work is published in the Journal of Animal Ecology.

mix_items.title: More time on social media means more anxiety, depression for teens—especially girls
mix_items.summary: Spending more time on social media is making Canadian teenagers—especially girls—feel anxious, depressed and disconnected, according to a study co-led by University of Alberta researchers.

mix_items.title: Cataract surgery continues to improve across Europe
mix_items.summary: A total of 363,039 cataract surgeries performed in 12 European countries in 2024 were recorded in the European Registry of Quality Outcomes for Cataract and Refractive Surgery (EUREQUO), according to the latest figures presented at the 44th Congress of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons (ESCRS).

mix_items.title: Lower breast, cervical cancer screening seen for adults with disabilities
mix_items.summary: Individuals with disabilities have a lower prevalence of breast and cervical cancer screening, according to a study published in Cancer.

mix_items.title: Nearly 10,000 patients reveal what works best for knee arthritis pain relief
mix_items.summary: A major analysis of 139 clinical trials involving nearly 10,000 people suggests that some of the simplest treatments may work best for knee osteoarthritis. Knee braces ranked highest overall for reducing pain, stiffness, and mobility problems, while water-based therapy was especially effective for pain and regular exercise consistently improved both pain and physical function. More high-tech approaches, including ultrasound, generally performed worse.

mix_items.title: Tiny cell “antennas” may help explain why some babies are born with heart defects
mix_items.summary: A newly discovered communication system in the microscopic “antennae” of cells may help explain how some congenital heart defects develop. When genetic mutations disrupt this system, the effects may extend beyond the heart to organs including the brain, kidneys, and skeleton.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
